Four symptoms, one root cause

Leadership raised it at an annual meeting. Users felt it every day. Each complaint traced back to how data got into the system.

Root causeUnreliable data entry

Open the interactive prototype
BeforeAfter

Old form

  • ~31 fields, mostly mandatory
  • Names typed by hand
  • Codes like EE and EN, unexplained

New request

  • 12 fields to start, the rest later
  • Names picked from lists
  • The system writes the request name

Designed for the unhappy paths too

Errors, exceptions and access needs were designed, not left for engineering to guess.

Edge cases

Data and validation

  • Duplicate or similar client names
  • Missing or dependent fields
  • Outdated and hidden list values

Workflow decisions

  • Conflicting Sales edits
  • Approve, correct or reject a name
  • Change owner, status or access

System and recovery

  • No results or empty periods
  • Loading, offline and partial failures
  • Save feedback, undo and retry

Accessibility

Color and contrast (WCAG 2.1 AA)

  • Text at least 4.5:1; large text 3:1
  • Controls and chart marks at least 3:1
  • Status never shown by color alone

Label clarity

  • Plain words instead of codes
  • Every field keeps a visible label
  • Errors say what’s wrong and how to fix it

Consistent wording

  • One name per action: New request, Owner, Hide option
  • Disabled fields explain why, like “Not needed”

Handoff

Rules I specified

  • Generated names and linked dropdowns
  • Status and outcome transitions
  • Admin review and preserved history

Dependencies to confirm

  • Teams and SharePoint channel creation
  • Email notifications and directory lookup
  • Data refresh and access permissions

Written for the build

The team builds with AI coding tools, so the specs spell out rules and states, not just frames.

This case study follows the same rules: it works with the keyboard alone, shows a visible focus ring, and turns motion off for anyone who asks their device to reduce it.

What changed after a five-day team beta

Five people used it for five days: 2 Sales, 2 Graphics and 1 Admin. I timed the same tasks before and after.

Weekly reporting, fully automated

Manual export and rebuild went from ~2–2.5 h to nothing. The dashboard is live.

Less admin effort

From hours of building reports to ~15 min reviewing new names.

Faster request creation

From ~10 min to ~6 min per request.

Duplicate client entries removed

A 26% leaner client list. Names are now picked, never typed.

Graphics work, visible for the first time

Every request now records what Graphics produced and how long it took. Before, none of this was tracked.

What this project taught me

I thought I was redesigning a dashboard. The real problem was how data got into it.

    Looking back

    Hardest trade-off
    Keeping the Graphics count whole, even when it didn’t add up at first glance.
    Feedback that changed me
    A new hire’s confusion made me rewrite every label.
    What comes next
    Formal task testing, and measuring results with more users.

    AI was my co-designer. The decisions were mine.

    I used AI to move faster and see more options. I set the direction, checked the output and made every call.

    What I owned

    • Framing the problem
    • Every design decision
    • Layouts that solve the user problem, on HTC’s design system

    Where AI sped me up

    • Sorting interview notes into themes
    • 6–8 layout variations in minutes
    • Clearer wording options
    • Checking files for spelling and missing screens

    How I stayed in control

    • Detailed briefs: main card, secondary card, layout flow
    • Read every synthesis line against the original feedback
    • Kept only what fit my reasoning

    Example: the three tabs

    My decision

    Split the request into Primary details, Supporting details and Graphics, so each role goes straight to its own fields.

    AI’s part

    Horizontal and vertical tab layouts: 6–8 low-fi variations in minutes.

    My call

    I reviewed each one and chose the layout that best supported the decision.

    Thanks for reading.
